fixes.explanation: The text says the spies “…brought out her whole family and settled them outside the camp of Israel.” (Joshua 6:23) So the word that matters here is outside. The spies brought out Rahab, her father and mother and brothers, and all who belonged to her. Inside the camp isn't where the text puts them.

The Moabites are another people, and they're not in this verse. Joshua 6:25 says, “So she has lived among the Israelites to this day.” That tells us where Rahab's life ended up, which is with Israel. The writer says it was still true as he wrote.

Yes. Joshua says, “at the cost of his firstborn he will lay its foundations; at the cost of his youngest he will set up its gates.” (Joshua 6:26) The oath is about the man who rises up and rebuilds Jericho. This one is heavy, so I'll just let it stand as written.

Yes. The text says, “So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame spread throughout the land.” (Joshua 6:27) Both things sit in that one verse. Joshua's name got around the whole land. I think the part to hold onto is the first one, that the LORD was with him.

Joshua asks, “Are You for us or for our enemies?” and the man answers, “Neither,” (Joshua 5:14). Then He says who He is: “I have now come as Commander of the LORD’s army.” So taking Israel's side isn't the answer He gives. I bet Joshua wasn't expecting that one.

The king of Jericho isn't who this is. The man tells Joshua, “I have now come as Commander of the LORD’s army.” (Joshua 5:14) Jericho's king comes up later, when the LORD says He has delivered the city into Joshua's hand, along with its king (Joshua 6:2). In this scene, Joshua falls facedown in reverence.

The Commander says, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy.” (Joshua 5:15) Then the text says, “And Joshua did so.” The order and the obeying sit right next to each other. Sandals off, and that's the whole scene.

Laying down a sword is a fair guess, since a drawn sword shows up right at the start, in the Commander's hand (Joshua 5:13). But the Commander never says anything to Joshua about a sword. He says, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy.” (Joshua 5:15) Sandals are the whole request.

Jericho's gates stay shut, actually. The text says, “Now Jericho was tightly shut up because of the Israelites. No one went out and no one came in.” (Joshua 6:1) That's a city sealed up tight. Nobody's even slipping out to check the mail.

Six days, one lap each. Then comes the seventh day: “…march around the city seven times, while the priests blow the horns.” (Joshua 6:4) Joshua 6:15 says that was the only day they circled seven times. Seven laps in one day? Somebody's getting their steps in.

Twice sounds like a gentle step up, but the LORD's plan is bigger. He says, “…on the seventh day, march around the city seven times, while the priests blow the horns.” (Joshua 6:4) Two laps would barely be a warm-up. Seven is the number.

Picture a parade with the ark in the middle. The text says, “…the armed troops marched ahead of the priests who blew the horns, and the rear guard followed the ark.” (Joshua 6:9) Troops, priests, ark, then the rear guard. I bet that spot at the back had a great view of the whole line.

Singing sounds nice, but Joshua's order is different: “Do not give a battle cry or let your voice be heard…” (Joshua 6:10) The text does have the horns sounding during the march (Joshua 6:9). The people are told to keep their voices quiet until the day he says to shout. That's a lot of holding it in.

Yes. The text says, “So he had the ark of the LORD carried around the city, circling it once. And the people returned to the camp and spent the night there.” (Joshua 6:11) One lap, then back to camp for the night. I'd have been tempted to ask if we were done yet.

This one is true, baker. Joshua 6:11 says, “And the people returned to the camp and spent the night there.” That comes right after the one lap around the city. I think it's easy to second-guess, since marching around a city feels like it should take longer.

Midnight is a fun guess, but the text says dawn. Joshua 6:15 says, “…they got up at dawn and marched around the city seven times in the same manner.” Dawn is when the day is just starting, not the middle of the night. Marching seven laps in the pitch dark would be a whole different kind of rough.

Joshua says, “Only Rahab the prostitute and all those with her in her house will live, because she hid the spies we sent.” (Joshua 6:17) The text gives her reason: she hid the spies. Everyone with her in her house is included. That's a house worth being in.

Tamar isn't named anywhere in this verse. Joshua says, “Only Rahab the prostitute and all those with her in her house will live…” (Joshua 6:17) The one he names is the woman who hid the spies. Tamar isn't part of what Joshua says here.

Deborah isn't named anywhere in this verse. Joshua names Rahab: “Only Rahab the prostitute and all those with her in her house will live…” (Joshua 6:17) The text says Rahab was spared because she hid the spies. Deborah isn't part of what Joshua says here.

Joshua tells “…the two men who had spied out the land…” to go into the house of the prostitute and bring out the woman and all who are with her. (Joshua 6:22) His words even include “…just as you promised her.” So the text shows the spies getting the job, and a promise to Rahab is part of the order. I think that fits nicely.

The priests do have a job in this passage: seven of them carry seven rams’ horns in front of the ark (Joshua 6:4). But Joshua gives this errand to someone else: “…the two men who had spied out the land…” (Joshua 6:22) The text doesn't send any priests to Rahab's house.
